idiom_name: IState interface + concrete state classes + context property
implementation_notes: The classic structure maps directly onto C#: an IState interface, one sealed class per state, and a context that holds the current state in a property and delegates; stateless states are exposed as static readonly singletons, so a transition is an ordinary property write with no allocation. An abstract base class is only worth adding when states share behaviour, and a switch expression over a record hierarchy is a legitimate data-oriented alternative, though only a sealed hierarchy gives the compiler exhaustiveness warnings. Keep this shape when states hold injected services or need reference identity.
pitfalls: Leaving state classes unsealed blocks the compiler from warning about unhandled states in switch expressions and invites accidental subclasses.
A static readonly state instance must be immutable; caching the current document inside a shared state object leaks state between documents.
Naming the property State collides with a state type or enum of the same name; renaming it (for example Phase) keeps call sites readable.
Writing the state property is not atomic with handling the event, so unsynchronised concurrent calls can interleave two transitions.

variants.name: Stateless state machine library
variants.implementation_notes: Stateless turns the pattern into configuration: the context owns a StateMachine<TState, TTrigger>, transitions are declared with Permit, side effects with OnEntry and OnExit, guards with PermitIf, and Fire(trigger) performs the transition while rejecting undefined (state, trigger) pairs. Reach for it when the graph must be introspectable (DOT or Mermaid export), when hierarchical or reentrant states, external state storage or parameterised triggers are needed, or when one graph is shared by several contexts; hand-written classes remain better when states are behavioural objects with dependencies.
pitfalls: The machine is mutable: give each context its own instance (or store the state externally via the StateAccessor overload) and do not Fire concurrently without synchronisation.
Entry and exit actions run synchronously inside Fire, so blocking work there stalls the caller and anything holding the machine's lock.
Configuration mistakes surface at runtime - Fire on an undeclared pair throws instead of failing at compile time, so cover the graph with tests.
